prompt.context: Rock Energy, an Oil & Gas company, is evaluating the purchase of one of three oil fields in Latin America. After purchasing the rights to extract oil from one of these fields, Rock Energy will outsource the drilling activity.
prompt.question: How would you evaluate the three oil fields, and which oil field should Rock Energy purchase?

clarifying_info.q: How long do the rights allow Rock Energy to operate?
clarifying_info.a: The rights give Rock Energy the right to drill during 1 year and produce oil for 20 years. Assume that no oil is produced until the beginning of year 2.

clarifying_info.q: How many rigs can be deployed?
clarifying_info.a: Rock Energy can get the drilling operator to deploy a maximum of 10 rigs in each of the regions.

clarifying_info.q: What does the cost of a rig day include?
clarifying_info.a: The cost of the rig day includes crew, consumables, and services.
Any amount of oil being extracted will be sold at the spot market price of the moment.

clarifying_info.q: What is the spot price of oil?
Are there maintenance costs during the production phase?
clarifying_info.a: For simplicity assume that the oil wells will produce the same amount of oil for the next 20 years with no maintenance costs.

clarifying_info.q: How much do the rights cost?
clarifying_info.a: The rights to extract oil cost $40M in each region.

exhibits.title: Oil Field Profiles, 2010
exhibits.shows: A table and bar charts comparing Region 1, Region 2, and Region 3 across drilling rates (meters/day), average depth of wells (meters), number of rigs, average well production (barrels per day), and cost per rig day.

framework: Estimate drilling time per well per region (depth / penetration rate)
Calculate cost per well (days to complete well x cost per rig day)
Calculate annual revenue per well (daily production x 360 days x spot price)
Calculate profit per well and profit margin per well
Determine number of wells drillable in one year per region (360 / days per well x 10 rigs)
Calculate total revenue, total cost (including $40M rights), and total profit per region
Compare regions quantitatively and select best investment
Assess qualitative risks: insurance, political stability, labor, oil price volatility, oil quality

questions.prompt: How many days does it take to drill one well in each region?
questions.guidance: Divide average depth by drilling rate (penetration rate). Region 1: 1200/20=60 days. Region 2: 2700/30=90 days. Region 3: 3600/20=180 days.

math.setup: Days per well = Average depth (meters) / Drilling rate (meters/day)
math.answer: Region 1 = 60 days, Region 2 = 90 days, Region 3 = 180 days

questions.prompt: What is the cost per well in each region?
questions.guidance: Multiply days per well by cost per rig day. Strong candidate notes that Region 3 is far more expensive per well.

math.setup: Cost per well = Days per well x Cost per rig day

questions.prompt: What is the yearly revenue per well in each region?
questions.guidance: Multiply daily production by 360 days and by the $50 spot price.

math.setup: Yearly revenue per well = Daily production (barrels/day) x 360 days x $50/barrel

questions.prompt: What is the profit per well and profit margin per well for each region?
questions.guidance: Profit per well = Revenue - Cost. Profit margin = Profit / Cost. Candidate should note Region 1 has the highest margin (500%) but this alone does not determine the best investment.

math.setup: Profit per well = Yearly revenue per well - Cost per well; Margin = Profit per well / Cost per well
math.answer: Region 1 profit/well = $1.5M (500% margin), Region 2 = $2.7M (300% margin), Region 3 = $1.8M (50% margin)

questions.prompt: How many wells can be drilled in one year per region (with 10 rigs)?
questions.guidance: Number of wells = (360 / days per well) x 10 rigs. Candidate must recognize that even though Region 3 has the highest per-well production, the long drilling time severely limits how many wells can be completed.

math.setup: Number of wells per year = (360 days / Days per well) x 10 rigs
math.answer: Region 1 = 60 wells, Region 2 = 40 wells, Region 3 = 20 wells

questions.prompt: What are the total revenue, total cost, and total profit for each region in the first year of production?
questions.guidance: Total revenue = yearly revenue per well x number of wells. Total cost = cost per well x number of wells + $40M rights. Profit = Total revenue - Total cost. Region 2 yields the highest profit despite having fewer wells than Region 1.

math.setup: Total revenue = (Revenue per well) x (Number of wells); Total cost = (Cost per well x Number of wells) + $40M; Profit = Total revenue - Total cost
steps: Region 1: Revenue = $1.8M x 60 = $108M; Cost = $300K x 60 + $40M = $18M + $40M = $58M; Profit = $108M - $58M = $50M
Region 2: Revenue = $3.6M x 40 = $144M; Cost = $900K x 40 + $40M = $36M + $40M = $76M; Profit = $144M - $76M = $68M
math.answer: Region 1 profit = $50M, Region 2 profit = $68M, Region 3 profit = -$4M

brainstorming.prompt: What qualitative factors and risks should Rock Energy consider before finalizing the investment decision?

categories.name: Political & Regulatory Risk
ideas: Political instability in the region could restrict access to well sites
Property rights may be insecure in certain jurisdictions
Nationalization or expropriation risk varies by country

categories.name: Insurance & Liability
ideas: Countries differ in required insurance coverage for Oil & Gas companies
Liability caps vary by country, affecting insurance costs significantly
Blowout or spill liability could exceed coverage in some regions

categories.name: Labor
ideas: Labor contracts and union presence differ by region
Labor costs and availability of skilled workers vary
Strikes or labor disputes could halt drilling operations

categories.name: Oil Price Volatility
ideas: Oil prices below $27/barrel would make all regions unprofitable
Spot price exposure for 20 years of production is significant
Hedging strategies may be needed to lock in future revenue

categories.name: Oil Quality
ideas: Differences in crude grade (light vs. heavy, sweet vs. sour) affect realized price
Lower-quality crude may trade at a discount to the $50 spot benchmark
Refinery compatibility could limit buyer pool

categories.name: Environmental & Operational
ideas: Environmental regulations and remediation obligations differ by country
Geological surprises could increase actual drilling time beyond estimates
Infrastructure (pipelines, ports) availability differs by region

recommendation: Rock Energy should purchase the rights to Region 2, which yields the highest first-year profit of $68M versus $50M for Region 1 and -$4M for Region 3

Although Region 1 has a higher per-well profit margin (500% vs. 300%), Region 2 generates significantly more total profit due to higher revenue per well, and the fixed $40M rights cost is spread over a comparable number of wells
Region 3 should be eliminated as it generates a loss under the current spot price and assumptions
risks: Oil prices below $27/barrel would make all regions unprofitable; Region 2 is not immune to price risk
Political instability or regulatory changes in the Region 2 country could disrupt operations
Actual drilling times may exceed estimates, reducing the number of wells completed in the first year
Oil quality differences could result in a lower realized price than the $50 benchmark
next_steps: Conduct due diligence on political stability, regulatory environment, and property rights in the Region 2 jurisdiction
Assess insurance requirements and obtain cost estimates for required coverage in Region 2
Explore hedging options (e.g., oil futures) to manage price volatility risk over the 20-year production horizon
Perform an expected value analysis assigning probabilities to different production outcomes per well to stress-test the $68M profit estimate
